sections.b: Job's go'el is the most debated use of the word. Abandoned by brothers, kin, servants and wife (Job 19:13–19), Job names a go'el, the role of the relative who rescues his kin: "As for me, I know that my redeemer lives, and at last he will stand up on the dust" (Job 19:25). The go'el's duties in the Law, to buy back land and people and to avenge blood (Leviticus 25:25, 47–49; Numbers 35:19), fit Job's situation: he has called on the earth not to cover his blood (Job 16:18) and wants his name cleared. Who the go'el is remains open. Most Jewish and many Christian interpreters say God, as in Isaiah, where the LORD is Israel's go'el (Isaiah 41:14; Isaiah 43:14). A major group of modern scholars (Mowinckel, Pope, Habel) sees instead the heavenly witness of Job 16:19, a defender in the divine council. Christian tradition, from the Greek and Latin translations and Handel's Messiah, hears the risen Christ. This site renders the word "my redeemer" in Job, lowercase, and "family redeemer" for Boaz.
sections.refs: Job 19:25–27; Job 19:13–19; Job 16:18–21; Leviticus 25:25; Leviticus 25:47–49; Numbers 35:19; Isaiah 41:14; Isaiah 43:14; Ruth 3:9

sections.h: The redeemer and the resurrection in Christian worship
sections.b: The Latin Vulgate made Job say "on the last day I will rise from the earth" (Job 19:25, Clementine Vulgate), and the verse entered the Office of the Dead, the Book of Common Prayer's burial service and the Catholic funeral readings. In 1741 Charles Jennens set it at the opening of Part III of Handel's Messiah, beside 1 Corinthians 15:20. Through these, "my Redeemer" became for English speakers a title of Christ as the one who rescues his own from death.

common: Christians widely read Job 19:25 as a prophecy of Christ the Redeemer and of the resurrection of the body.
uncommon: Clines holds that Job's go'el is not a person at all but Job's own cry and testimony, personified as the witness is in Job 16:19–20.

sections.b: In the second round each friend paints the fate of the wicked: Eliphaz the man who lives in dread (Job 15), Bildad the man caught in traps and forgotten (Job 18), Zophar the man who swallows riches and vomits them up (Job 20). Job speaks past them. He describes God as an enemy who has torn him (Job 16:9–14), calls on the earth to keep his blood uncovered and names a witness in heaven (Job 16:18–21), asks God to stand bail for him (Job 17:3), and declares, when everyone has abandoned him, that his redeemer lives (Job 19:25–27). The round ends with his reply from experience: the wicked often prosper and are buried in honor (Job 21).

sections.h: The friends' poems and Job's facts (Job 15–21)
sections.b: The second round of Job is the Bible's fullest debate about retribution. Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar each describe the fate of the wicked: inner dread, traps, disease, childlessness, loss of name, wealth vomited up (Job 15:20–35; Job 18:5–21; Job 20:4–29). Their teaching is the teaching of much of Proverbs and the Psalms. Job answers with what anyone can see: the wicked live long, their children prosper, they die in an instant and are buried with honor (Job 21:7–33). He also rejects the idea that God punishes a man's children instead of him (Job 21:19–21), a debate that Jeremiah and Ezekiel also took up (Jeremiah 31:29–30; Ezekiel 18).

common: Job 21 is often read as the Bible's strongest statement that the wicked can prosper to the end of their lives.

sections.b: At his lowest point Job pictures Sheol as his house, where he will make his bed in the dark, call the Pit his father and the maggot his mother and sister (Job 17:13–14). His hope goes down with him to "the bars of Sheol" (Job 17:16). Bildad pictures Death's firstborn and "the king of terrors" (Job 18:13–14), and Job says the wicked go down to Sheol in an instant, without pain (Job 21:13).

In Job 16:9 Job says of God, "he holds a grudge against me", using satam, a close relative of satan, "to oppose, accuse". Job, who never sees the heavenly scenes of chapters 1–2, gives God the role the Accuser played there. He also says God's hand has "touched" him (Job 19:21), the verb the Accuser used (Job 1:11; Job 2:5).
sections.refs: Job 16:9; Job 30:21; Job 19:21; Job 1:11; Job 2:5; Genesis 27:41

sections.b: Eliphaz asks Job, "Were you a listener at God's council?" (Job 15:8). The reader has seen that council meet (Job 1:6; Job 2:1), but no human in the book has. Some scholars think Job's witness in heaven (Job 16:19) and his redeemer (Job 19:25) are members of the same council, who would take his side.
sections.refs: Job 15:8; Job 1:6; Job 2:1; Job 16:19; Job 19:25; Jeremiah 23:18

sections.h: "From my flesh I will see God" (Job 19:26)
sections.b: Job's deepest hope is to see God for himself, "my own eyes will see, and not a stranger" (Job 19:27). Whether he means in the body ("from within my flesh") or apart from it ("without my flesh") is debated. In the end he says he has seen God (Job 42:5). Christians link the hope with seeing God at the resurrection (1 John 3:2; Matthew 5:8).

sections.h: A witness who pleads for Job (Job 16:19–21)
sections.b: Job hopes for a witness in heaven who will "plead for a man before God, as a mortal does for his friend" (Job 16:21), and asks God to stand bail for him (Job 17:3). The figure may be God himself, a heavenly advocate, or Job's own cry. Christian readers see Christ, who intercedes for us (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1).
sections.refs: Job 16:19–21; Job 17:3; Job 9:33; Job 33:23; Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1

sections.b: Eliphaz grounds wisdom in tradition: what wise men received from their fathers, in a land no outsider walked through (Job 15:17–19). Job answers with experience: ask the travelers, and they will tell you the wicked are spared (Job 21:29–30). The book sets the two kinds of wisdom against each other.

Job's speeches in the second round use the language of the lament psalms and Lamentations: God as an enemy archer and besieger, sackcloth and dust, enemies gaping and striking the cheek, friends and family turned away (Job 16:9–16; Job 19:7–20; compare Lamentations 3:1–13; Psalm 88:8). Unlike most laments, they end not in praise but in a legal hope: a witness and a redeemer.

The Greek translation makes Job 19:26 say that God will "raise up my skin", and the Latin Vulgate has "on the last day I will rise from the earth". 1 Clement 26:3, Jerome and most church fathers read the passage as a prophecy of bodily resurrection, and it is read at Christian funerals. The Hebrew is harder: "after my skin has been stripped off... from my flesh I will see God" can mean in the body or without it, and many modern scholars read it as a hope that God will clear Job's name. The Talmud records the view that Job denied the resurrection, citing Job 7:9 (Bava Batra 16a).

In the second round the friends stop urging Job to repent and describe the fate of the wicked in poems that fit Job's own losses: Eliphaz's man in dread (Job 15), Bildad's trapped and childless man who "does not know God" (Job 18:21), Zophar's glutton who vomits up his riches (Job 20). They do not answer Job's appeal to a witness in heaven or his confession of a living redeemer. Job calls them "comforters who bring trouble" (Job 16:2) and ends the round by calling their answers faithlessness (Job 21:34).

Job cries "Violence!", the legal cry for help, and no one answers, because the one he accuses is the judge (Job 19:7). He wants his words engraved as testimony (Job 19:23–24), hopes for a witness and a go'el who will stand up for him, and warns the friends that there is a judgment (Job 19:29).

sections.h: The cup of the Almighty's fury (Job 21:20)
sections.b: Job wants the wicked man himself, not his children, to "drink down the Almighty's fury" (Job 21:20), using the prophets' picture of God's anger as a cup. Zophar pictures God raining his burning anger on the glutton as his meal (Job 20:23).
